alternatives.consequence: This is the preferred reconciliation: confirmation remains expected without a request, while demonstration to the SFC’s satisfaction is request-triggered.

alternatives.condition: The footnote’s unqualified instruction to confirm and demonstrate has independent operative effect.
alternatives.consequence: Demonstration of its minimum matters remains expected without a request. This supported rival does not remove the separate express request conditions for obtaining external assurance or a legal opinion.

alternatives.condition: The request qualification extends across both coordinated verbs.
alternatives.consequence: Neither confirmation nor demonstration would be activated by that sentence without a request. This is a weaker grammatical reading and faces the footnote’s unqualified wording; it does not suspend independent substantive responsibilities.

alternatives.condition: The SFC-satisfaction phrase attaches only to demonstration, as its immediate placement suggests.
alternatives.consequence: Requested demonstration must satisfy the SFC, but confirmation is not expressly subject to a separate prior acceptance decision. An inaccurate or unsupported confirmation is not thereby sufficient.

alternatives.condition: The SFC-satisfaction phrase supplies a shared standard for confirmation and demonstration.
alternatives.consequence: Both acts concern matters subject to that standard. This supported broader reading does not itself establish a prior-approval or unsolicited-submission procedure.

alternatives.condition: High confidence attaches locally to the smart-contract security proposition.

alternatives.condition: High confidence qualifies the combined compliance-and-security showing.

value.conclusion:
The preferred reading separates confirmation from request-triggered demonstration. The request qualification appears after the conjunction and immediately before demonstration, so Product Providers should confirm without awaiting an SFC request and, upon request, demonstrate to the SFC’s satisfaction. Both verbs share the same objects: management and operational soundness of the tokenisation arrangement, record keeping of ownership, and integrity of the smart contracts. Demonstration is not confined to smart-contract integrity. The satisfaction standard attaches most directly to demonstration; applying it to both coordinated acts remains a supported, less direct reading.

The accompanying footnote expressly identifies the SFC as recipient of confirmation and demonstration and supplies minimum substantive content: compliance with the incorporated operational requirements and a high-confidence showing that smart contracts are not subject to contract vulnerabilities or security flaws. High confidence most naturally qualifies the smart-contract security proposition, although attachment to the combined compliance-and-security showing is possible. It expresses confidence in the security proposition, not a restriction to particularly severe flaws. It does not supply a numerical threshold, guarantee against future flaws, or substitute for the SFC-satisfaction standard.

The strongest reconciliation treats the footnote as elaborating substance while preserving the main sentence’s express request condition. On that reading, no SFC request leaves confirmation expected but does not activate the specified demonstration requirement. However, the footnote’s unqualified repetition of confirmation and demonstration supports a genuine rival under which demonstration is independently expected. Reading the request qualification as covering both acts is grammatically weaker but cannot be conclusively excluded. None of these readings creates a general exemption from the underlying substantive responsibilities.

The neighbouring procurement requirements differ from the Provider’s own confirmation and demonstration. One expressly calls, upon SFC request, for third-party audit or verification concerning the same operational, ownership-record and smart-contract matters. Audit or verification are textual alternatives, not an express requirement to obtain both; the sentence does not repeat the SFC-satisfaction standard. The other expressly calls, upon request, for a satisfactory legal opinion supporting the application. Its application-supporting purpose is established, but its precise legal questions and the evaluator of satisfaction are unspecified. Neither procurement requirement expressly substitutes for the other or for confirmation and requested demonstration. A demonstration request does not automatically activate both procurement requirements; the communication’s actual scope matters.

Without the relevant requests, those procurement requirements are not activated by their own wording. That does not mean no assessment or assurance can otherwise be needed: the supplied technical appendix conditionally contemplates technology audits, smart-contract audits and justified reliance on third-party work. Product Providers retain ultimate responsibility despite outsourcing. Proper ownership records, operational compatibility, risk controls, recovery arrangements, robust business continuity and additional proper controls for public-permissionless networks remain substantive expectations. Confirmation, procurement, submission or recorded supervision does not alone establish those outcomes or SFC satisfaction. The wording states regulatory expectations using ‘should’; it does not itself establish a freestanding statutory liability rule or prove actual compliance, breach or regulatory acceptance.

5 Product Providers should confirm and demonstrate to the SFC that, at a minimum, they comply with the requirements as set out in paragraphs 10 to 13 above and the smart contracts are not subject to any contract vulnerabilities or security flaws with a high level of confidence.

Product Providers should, upon SFC’s request, obtain third party audit or verification on the management and operational soundness of the tokenisation arrangement, record keeping of ownership and integrity of the smart contracts.
Product Providers should, upon SFC’s request, obtain satisfactory legal opinion to support its application.

Product Providers should remain and be ultimately responsible for the management and operational soundness of the tokenisation arrangement adopted and record keeping of ownership, regardless of any outsourcing arrangement1.

Product Providers should ensure that proper records of token holders’ ownership interests in the product are maintained and the tokenisation arrangement is operationally compatible with service providers involved2.

Product Providers should have appropriate measures in place to manage and mitigate cybersecurity risks3, data privacy, system outages and recovery, and maintain a comprehensive and robust business continuity plan.
Product Providers should not use public-permissionless blockchain networks without additional and proper controls (eg, Product Providers to impose additional control by using a permissioned token)4.

1 Given that these tokenised products are offered to the public in Hong Kong and the importance of maintaining proper records to reflect investors’ ownership, the Product Provider should remain fully responsible, despite any outsourcing arrangement such as those envisaged under 6.8 of the Code on Unit Trusts and Mutual Funds. For factors of consideration, please also refer to Part A of the Appendix to the Tokenised Securities Circular, where applicable, when formulating the tokenisation arrangement.

By adopting a see-through approach, the SFC is of the view that it is appropriate to allow primary dealing of tokenised SFC-authorised investment products, as long as the underlying product can meet all the applicable product authorisation requirements and the additional safeguards to address the new risks associated with the tokenisation arrangement (as set out in paragraphs 10-19 below).

Product providers of tokenised SFC-authorised investment products (Product Providers) should ensure that the underlying products should meet the applicable requirements in the relevant rules and regulations, and product codes (including eligibility of Product Providers, product structure, investment and operational requirements, disclosure and ongoing compliance obligations).

Additional requirements set out below, as well as the relevant requirements in the Circular on intermediaries engaging in tokenised securities-related activities issued by the SFC (Tokenised Securities Circular), should also be satisfied.

Chapter 1: Preliminary
      Introduction to the Handbook

1.1   The Handbook is made under section 399 of the SFO and establishes codes or
      guidelines for the authorization of products covered by the Handbook and their offering
      documents and advertisements. These guidelines are not intended to be exhaustive.

1.2   Section I of the Handbook sets out the high-level principles and requirements that are
      intended to apply to all products. More detailed product-specific requirements applicable
      to specific types of products are contained in the applicable product code.

1.3   The Handbook provides general guidelines for authorization of products specifically
      stated in the applicable product codes. The Commission will have regard to both the
      spirit as well as the letter of the General Principles set out in Chapter 3 of this
      Overarching Principles Section in considering products authorization applications and
      whether products should remain authorized.

1.4   All products, their Product Providers and the Specified Entities are expected to comply
      with all applicable principles and requirements set out in Section I of the Handbook in
      addition to the detailed product-specific requirements applicable to specific types of
      products that are contained in the applicable product code.

1.5   The Handbook does not have the force of law and shall not be interpreted in a way that
      will override the provision of any law.

unresolved: The footnote’s unqualified repetition of demonstration creates genuine tension with the main sentence’s express request condition. Harmonisation favours preserving that condition, but the independent-demonstration rival remains supported.

The wording does not conclusively settle shared attachment of the SFC-satisfaction standard or the breadth of the high-confidence qualification. It specifies no precise deadline, frequency or unsolicited-submission procedure for independent confirmation, and no exhaustive evidentiary method for either standard.

The qualifications attached to ownership records and operational compatibility, and to cybersecurity measures, are not delivered. The network-control cross-reference is delivered, but the referenced intermediary discussion of network risks is absent. These gaps limit a complete account of the incorporated substantive requirements, not the bounded grammatical comparison.

The supplied technical appendix supports conditional consideration of audits, technical resilience, interoperability, operational controls and legal issues. It is incomplete and carries an extraction qualification. Its intermediary-facing language and the Provider’s direction to consider applicable factors do not establish a universal mandatory audit procedure or a sufficient-compliance safe harbour.

No actual SFC request, confirmation, demonstration, assurance report, legal opinion or regulatory assessment is supplied. Request scope and timing, report coverage, methods, exceptions, remediation and the underlying operational evidence would distinguish fulfilment from mere procurement or submission.

The legal-opinion sentence establishes an application-supporting purpose, but does not specify the opinion’s exact legal questions, author qualifications or whose satisfaction governs. Those matters cannot be inferred from the operational-assurance sentence alone.

The supplied Handbook distinguishes regulatory and evidential consequences from automatic liability for breach and states that authorisation does not establish compliance with all applicable requirements. Product-specific conditions or actual modifications remain unchecked; merely imaginable outside exceptions are not prerequisites to this textual answer.

1.11   The SFC takes no responsibility for the contents of any offering documents or
